claims.text: Transition-metal catalytic activity is governed by the position of the d-band center.
The d-band center dictates the adsorption energies of key reaction intermediates.
A pure transition-metal catalyst such as Ni or Co can provide a baseline with a well-characterized d-band center.
Incorporating a second transition metal can shift the host catalyst's d-band center.
The dopant level can be selected so that the d-band center shifts without significantly altering catalyst morphology.
Using identical temperature, pressure, feed composition, and electrolyte conditions ensures that only electronic structure differs between samples.
Dopant incorporation modifies the catalyst electronic structure by shifting the d-band center.
A shift in the d-band center changes the binding energies of reaction intermediates.
An optimal d-band-center shift improves intermediate adsorption and desorption kinetics.
Improved adsorption and desorption kinetics enhance catalytic activity and may alter selectivity.
Electronic-structure modification may eventually impose limits on catalyst durability.
A moderately shifted d-band center will produce higher catalytic activity, such as higher turnover frequency, than the undoped baseline.
An excessive d-band-center shift can cause intermediates to bind too strongly or too weakly.
Overbinding or underbinding caused by an excessive shift can harm selectivity or durability.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply when particle size, crystallinity, morphology, and reaction conditions are controlled.
Morphological deviations or extreme operating conditions may introduce effects other than the proposed electronic-structure mechanism.
The precise d-band-center shift that maximizes performance is unknown.
A lack of correlation between measured d-band-center changes and catalytic performance changes would falsify the proposed governing relationship.
